questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'A blessing in disguise'
options: Something that seems bad but turns out beneficial
A hidden treasure discovered unexpectedly
An unfortunate accident with no silver lining
A dangerous situation with an uncertain outcome
questions.explanation: A blessing in disguise = something that initially appears negative but ultimately brings a good result. Example: Losing the first job was a blessing in disguise; it led him to a better career.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Hit the nail on the head'
options: Cause accidental damage to something nearby
Say or do exactly the right thing
Work extremely hard on a challenging task
Make a serious error of judgment
questions.explanation: Hit the nail on the head = describe or identify something exactly correctly. Example: Your analysis of the problem hit the nail on the head.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Once in a blue moon'
options: Every night when the moon is visible
During a special lunar phenomenon
Very rarely; on infrequent occasions
Exactly once every calendar month
questions.explanation: Once in a blue moon = something that happens very rarely or infrequently. A 'blue moon' is a rare second full moon in a calendar month, hence the idiom for rarity.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Bite the bullet'
options: React aggressively to a dangerous attack
Fight with exceptional courage in battle
Win a difficult contest through persistence
Endure a painful or difficult situation stoically
questions.explanation: Bite the bullet = accept and endure something unpleasant or difficult without complaining. Origin: soldiers bit on a bullet during surgery before anaesthesia. Example: Just bite the bullet and pay the repair bill.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Burn the midnight oil'
options: Work or study very late into the night
Waste precious resources carelessly
Light a fire to keep warm at midnight
Perform dangerous work in total darkness
questions.explanation: Burn the midnight oil = work or study late into the night. Origin: before electricity, people used oil lamps; working past midnight meant burning extra oil. Example: She burned the midnight oil to finish her thesis.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Let the cat out of the bag'
options: Release a trapped or confined animal
Accidentally reveal a secret or surprise
Create confusion by introducing chaos
Make a careless mistake in a critical moment
questions.explanation: Let the cat out of the bag = accidentally disclose a secret. Origin: refers to the old market trick of substituting a cat for a pig in a sack; the trick was exposed when the cat escaped.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'The ball is in your court'
options: A favourable sporting situation has developed
The problem has been successfully resolved
It is now your turn to take a decision or action
You are currently winning the competition
questions.explanation: The ball is in your court = it is your responsibility or turn to act or decide. Derived from tennis, where the ball crosses to the opponent's side. Example: I've made my offer; the ball is in your court now.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Beat around the bush'
options: Search the forest for a hidden object
Play games in an open outdoor area
Hunt animals through dense undergrowth
Avoid coming to the main point directly
questions.explanation: Beat around the bush = talk around a subject without addressing it directly; avoid the main point. Origin: hunting practice of beating bushes to scare out game before addressing it. Example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me the truth.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Spill the beans'
options: Reveal secret or confidential information
Waste food items through carelessness
Create a messy and disorderly situation
Drop objects accidentally and carelessly
questions.explanation: Spill the beans = disclose secret information, often accidentally. Origin: possibly from ancient Greece, where voting was done with beans and spilling them revealed the result early. Example: Who spilled the beans about the surprise party?
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Cost an arm and a leg'
options: Result in a serious physical injury
Be extremely expensive or overpriced
Demand an enormous amount of effort
Take an unreasonably long period of time
questions.explanation: Cost an arm and a leg = be very expensive. The idiom equates the price to something as precious as a limb. Example: The repairs to the car cost an arm and a leg.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Break the ice'
options: Shatter a barrier blocking a water channel
Begin a dangerous and challenging activity
Initiate conversation to ease an awkward situation
Overcome a major obstacle through persistence
questions.explanation: Break the ice = do or say something to relieve tension or awkwardness in a social situation. Origin: refers to the practice of sending ice-breaking ships ahead to clear a path. Example: He told a joke to break the ice at the meeting.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Bite off more than one can chew'
options: Consume an excessively large amount of food
Take an unnecessarily dangerous personal risk
Lose one's patience in a frustrating situation
Take on a responsibility too great to handle
questions.explanation: Bite off more than one can chew = take on a task or commitment that is beyond one's capacity. Example: She bit off more than she could chew by accepting three projects simultaneously.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Under the weather'
options: Feeling ill or not in good health
Standing exposed to heavy rainfall
Feeling sad about unfavourable weather
Working outdoors in difficult conditions
questions.explanation: Under the weather = feeling slightly ill or unwell. Nautical origin: sailors feeling sick would go below deck, literally under the weather side of the ship. Example: I won't be coming in today; I'm feeling a bit under the weather.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Miss the boat'
options: Arrive too late at a harbour or port
Fail to take advantage of an opportunity
Make an error while planning a voyage
Lose one's sense of direction entirely
questions.explanation: Miss the boat = fail to take advantage of an opportunity because one acted too late. Example: He missed the boat by not buying shares when the price was low.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Hit the sack'
options: Win decisively in a competitive contest
Attack someone without prior warning
Go to bed and sleep for the night
Pack one's belongings in preparation to leave
questions.explanation: Hit the sack = go to bed. 'Sack' is informal for bed, derived from the days when mattresses were sacks filled with straw. Example: It is already midnight; I need to hit the sack.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Barking up the wrong tree'
options: Making unnecessary noise in a quiet space
Searching for something in a risky location
Pursuing a wrong or mistaken course of action
Disturbing wild animals in their natural habitat
questions.explanation: Barking up the wrong tree = making a wrong assumption; blaming or pursuing the wrong person or direction. Origin: a hunting dog barking at the base of a tree where the quarry is no longer present. Example: If you suspect me, you're barking up the wrong tree.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'A drop in the ocean'
options: Something very deep below the surface
A modest but promising beginning
Part of an extremely large collection
A very small and insignificant contribution
questions.explanation: A drop in the ocean = a very small amount compared to what is needed or what exists. Example: The ₹1,000 donated was just a drop in the ocean compared to the ₹10 crore required for relief.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Cut corners'
options: Do something in the cheapest way, sacrificing quality
Take a shorter route while travelling on roads
Damage furniture or property through carelessness
Work at great speed to finish before a deadline
questions.explanation: Cut corners = do something in the easiest, fastest, or cheapest way, often compromising quality or omitting important steps. Example: The contractor cut corners on the construction, which caused structural damage later.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Burning bridges'
options: Destroying physical infrastructure during conflict
Damaging relationships so they cannot be repaired
Crossing dangerous rivers at great personal risk
Taking extreme and irreversible drastic measures
questions.explanation: Burning bridges = permanently damaging a relationship or eliminating the possibility of returning to a previous situation. Origin: armies burned bridges to prevent retreat or enemy advance. Example: Quitting without notice was burning bridges with that employer.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Kill two birds with one stone'
options: Become highly skilled in a competitive sport
Complete a repetitive task in half the usual time
Accomplish two things with a single action or effort
Waste effort by attempting multiple tasks together
questions.explanation: Kill two birds with one stone = accomplish two tasks or goals with a single action. Example: By meeting the client during his business trip, he killed two birds with one stone.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Throw in the towel'
options: Clean up and tidy an area after a contest
Begin a new initiative with great enthusiasm
Make a fresh attempt after an initial failure
Give up or concede defeat in a contest
questions.explanation: Throw in the towel = admit defeat and stop trying. Boxing origin: a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop a fight when their boxer cannot continue. Example: After three failed attempts, he threw in the towel.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'On the fence'
options: Situated at the boundary of two properties
Undecided or neutral between two positions
Physically elevated above the ground level
Keeping a careful watch over a situation
questions.explanation: On the fence = unable or unwilling to commit to a position or decision; remaining neutral. Example: He was on the fence about which political party to support in the election.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Get out of hand'
options: Become impossible to control or manage
Escape from physical captivity or restraint
Leave an unpleasant situation with great speed
Lose one's grip on a held object accidentally
questions.explanation: Get out of hand = become uncontrollable or beyond management. Example: The minor argument got out of hand and turned into a serious dispute. Antonym phrase: 'in hand' (under control).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Throw caution to the wind'
options: Give careful and considered advice to colleagues
Worry excessively about every minor possibility
Take all necessary precautions before proceeding
Act recklessly by ignoring all risks or warnings
questions.explanation: Throw caution to the wind = act recklessly; disregard all warnings and proceed without care. Example: Throwing caution to the wind, he invested his entire savings in one startup.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Put all your eggs in one basket'
options: Be extremely careful with limited resources
Save everything diligently for the distant future
Risk everything on a single plan or outcome
Gather and organise all assets in one location
questions.explanation: Put all your eggs in one basket = risk all resources on a single venture; not diversify. If the basket drops, all eggs break. Example: Investing only in one company is putting all your eggs in one basket.
questions.subject: English
